stories.headline: Vijay Pande's new AI-biotech fund makes five concentrated bets a year, not 30
stories.dek: After running $4 billion at a16z, the investor is betting that AI-driven medicine requires deep founder relationships and shared data infrastructure, not portfolio spread.
stories.summary:
Vijay Pande, who built a16z's biotech practice into a $4 billion operation, left to co-found VZVC with investor Zach Werner. The new firm deliberately constrains itself to roughly five investments yearly rather than dozens, operates without associates, and leans on AI agents for operations—treating each company addition as "wanting to have another child" rather than a quick social-media-style add.

Pande frames the shift within a larger thesis: AI is moving biology from a science of serendipitous discovery toward something engineered. Machine learning can now identify drug targets, design compounds, optimize clinical trials, and support precision medicine by personalizing treatment to individual biology rather than population averages. The key constraint is data. Unlike language models, which train on freely available text, biomedical AI can't scrape the internet—every company builds proprietary datasets.

This creates a paradox. Open-source foundation models in biology are emerging as powerful alternatives to corporate ones, much like open LLMs competed successfully against closed versions. Pande sees the future in biological atlases and shared infrastructure, not walled gardens. The real bottleneck to AI's promise in medicine isn't technology or talent; it's whether the field will cooperate enough to generate training data at scale, and whether founder-investor relationships can survive the 5-10 year timescales required to move from research to market impact.
stories.why_it_matters: For your consulting practice, this illustrates how AI adoption in regulated, data-scarce domains diverges sharply from the large-scale, quick-scaling patterns that work in consumer software. For your teaching, Pande's framework for engineering-oriented biotech is a concrete alternative to the "AI solves everything" narrative—one grounded in realistic trial economics, animal-model failures, and data scarcity. For India's ecosystem, his emphasis on open foundation models and shared atlases over proprietary data moats suggests how emerging biotech sectors can leapfrog by prioritizing interoperable infrastructure from the start.
stories.potential_use: Use Pande's shift from portfolio breadth to founder depth as a teaching case: what does AI-driven business model design look like when you can't rely on scale economies? Also, the biological-data problem is directly applicable to India's growing clinical research sector—a workshop could explore how Indian biotech can build competitive advantage through open infrastructure and federated data governance rather than race-to-proprietary-dataset dynamics.

sources.title: “We’re not doing 30 bets a year”: Vijay Pande on betting small after running $4 billion at a16z

stories.headline: Nvidia's next infrastructure edge isn't raw compute—it's data orchestration
stories.dek: The company's new Vera CPU achieves 3x efficiency gains by solving the hard problem of moving data at scale, not just processing it faster.
stories.summary:
Nvidia's earnings week revealed a subtle but significant shift in how the company is defending its dominance. While rivals like Amazon and Google have built custom GPUs, Nvidia has quietly built expertise across the entire data center stack—CPUs for memory management, networking systems, and storage orchestration designed specifically to work together.

The technical problem is real and increasingly urgent: as AI workloads scale into the gigawatt range, the bottleneck isn't the GPU anymore—it's moving data efficiently enough to keep those GPUs fed. Nvidia's Vera CPU, paired with the new Rubin GPU architecture, handles this through intelligent data traffic control. According to Jason Hardy, Nvidia's VP of storage technology, these systems achieve upwards of 3x efficiency improvements by preventing data movement bottlenecks that would otherwise starve compute resources.

This mirrors a pattern elsewhere in the industry. OpenAI's Jalapeño chip, for instance, took a different approach: minimize data movement entirely by fitting entire workloads into a single integrated chip. But the underlying insight is identical—systems-level efficiency now matters more than raw processor speed. That opens a new competitive layer where the real advantage goes to whoever can orchestrate the whole system, not just build the fastest piece of it. At this stage, Nvidia has built the most complete toolkit.
stories.why_it_matters: For an AI consultancy and educator, this is crucial: your clients won't win by scaling raw compute—they'll win by understanding how to architect efficient data pipelines around their infrastructure. The economics of enterprise AI applications depend on whether you can run them at acceptable tokens-per-watt, which Nvidia is now addressing through systems design rather than chip performance alone. This represents a real shift in how to think about AI infrastructure costs and constraints at scale.
stories.potential_use: For workshops, this is a concrete frame: teach the progression from compute-focused to orchestration-focused infrastructure thinking, using Vera's 3x efficiency gains as a tangible example of why data movement and memory architecture matter. For consulting, position data orchestration strategy as a distinct service—helping clients evaluate whether their infrastructure stack (regardless of chip vendor) is actually optimized for their workload's data patterns, not just its compute needs.

sources.title: Nvidia’s AI advantage is moving beyond the GPU
